symbols.name: rho_i(T)
symbols.meaning: density of ice (mass of ice per unit volume of ice)

symbols.name: D(phi, T)
symbols.meaning: effective diffusivity of water vapor through the pore gas, per unit total cross-section (includes the gas fraction, tortuosity and any Knudsen correction; tends to 0 in the ice)

steps.title: Water mass per unit volume
steps.why: Water is present as ice in the fraction $\phi$ and as vapor in the gas fraction $1-\phi$; $\rho_v$ is per unit gas volume, so it is weighted by $1-\phi$.

steps.title: Integral conservation of water
steps.why: Water is neither created nor destroyed; in a fixed control volume its mass changes only by the flux through the boundary. Ice does not move (A3), so only vapor carries water across $\partial\Omega$.
steps.operation: conservation of mass over a fixed control volume

check.printed: Statement of the conservation principle; nothing to compute.

steps.title: Fickian vapor flux
steps.why: With no bulk gas flow (A4), vapor moves by diffusion down its density gradient; $D$ is an effective diffusivity per unit total area that depends on $\phi$ and $T$ and vanishes in the ice.

check.printed: d_x(D d_x rho_v) has units kilogram / meter ** 3 / second, the same as d_t((1-phi) rho_v)

steps.title: Local form
steps.why: The divergence theorem turns the surface integral into a volume integral; the volume is fixed and arbitrary and the fields are smooth (A1), so the integrand vanishes pointwise.

check.printed: S4 int of div J = 0 (1D divergence-theorem test)

steps.title: Exchange term made explicit
steps.why: Splitting into a vapor balance and an ice balance shows the sublimation source $\sigma = -\partial_t(\phi\rho_i)$ that the ice loses and the vapor gains; with constant $\rho_i$ this is $-\rho_i\partial_t\phi$, and the vapor equation reads $(1-\phi)\partial_t\rho_v + (\rho_i-\rho_v)\partial_t\phi - \nabla\cdot(D\nabla\rho_v)=0$.
steps.operation: split into ice and vapor balances, define $\sigma$

steps.title: Residual in 3D Cartesian coordinates
steps.why: Write the divergence and gradient of S4 component by component; R is the left side of S4.

check.printed: S5 R expanded printed in full; every term has units kg m^-3 s^-1 (check_units)

assumptions_used: A1: $\phi$ and $T$ are known, smooth fields (given).

A2: The pore space holds only ice and gas, so the volume fractions are $\phi$ and $1-\phi$; $\rho_v$ is per unit gas volume and the ice density $\rho_i(T)$ is per unit ice volume. Grains of regolith are excluded from the domain (or enter only through $D$).
A3: Ice is rigid and does not move; it gains or loses water only by deposition and sublimation.
A4: The gas has no bulk (advective or Stefan) flow; vapor moves only by diffusion.
A5: Vapor diffusion obeys Fick's law with an effective diffusivity $D(\phi,T)$ per unit total area, which includes the gas fraction, tortuosity and any Knudsen correction and goes to zero in ice.

neglected.effect: Advection of vapor by bulk gas flow, including Stefan flow caused by sublimation
neglected.why: Vapor is a trace species or the gas is rarefied; the Stefan velocity is about $\sigma/\rho_{gas}$ and gives a Peclet number $vL/D\ll 1$ at pore scale ($L\sim10^{-5}$ m).
The Soret coefficient for water in air is about $10^{-3}$ K$^{-1}$ or smaller, so it is small next to the Fickian flux from the much steeper dependence of saturation density on $T$.

neglected.effect: Surface diffusion of adsorbed water on grains and ice
neglected.why: Adsorbed mass on the grains is not part of the model; its flux is small next to gas-phase transport for pore sizes much larger than the adsorbed layer.

neglected.effect: Motion and creep of the ice
neglected.why: Ice creep velocities at 200 K are many orders of magnitude slower than sublimation fronts.
Kept in the result through $\rho_i(T)$; ice thermal expansion is about $1.5\times10^{-4}$ K$^{-1}$, so setting $\rho_i$ constant changes the result by under 0.1% per 10 K if a later task wants it.

neglected.effect: Water bound in or adsorbed on regolith grains
neglected.why: Outside the ice-gas pore model by the statement.
